items.title: User–AI–Physician Collaboration in Self-Medication: Decision Weight Allocation and Continuance Intention
items.abstract: Self-medication increasingly involves artificial intelligence (AI) and healthcare professionals, yet how users distribute decision authority among AI, physicians, and themselves remains insufficiently understood. This study examined decision-authority allocation and continuance intention in user–AI–physician self-medication systems among 1136 participants. Measures included perceived eHealth literacy, AI use, perceived AI risk, trust, self-medication behavior, and fixed-sum authority allocations. Participants assigned the greatest authority to physicians, followed by AI and themselves, and preferred joint AI–physician systems over either single-agent configuration. Higher eHealth literacy was associated with more frequent AI use, lower perceived risk, greater trust, more authority allocated to AI and users, and less physician-reliant behavior. Trust in AI and physicians showed distinct associations with authority allocation and system preference, while autonomous self-medication behavior was related to authority allocation. These findings conceptualize digital self-medication as a triadic process and support adaptive designs that coordinate roles, preserve user agency, and mitigate AI overreliance.

items.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to Help Human Commanders Fight Future Indo-Pacific Wars
items.abstract: Military forces are beginning to use artificial intelligence (AI) in warfighting. One of the first AI uses is in decision support systems (DSSs), computerised tools that assist commanders in understanding the battlefield, planning future courses of action and directing their forces. The use of such AI-enabled DSSs by humans creates a shared cognition. The use of DSSs in Gaza and Ukraine has revealed both their strengths and shortcomings, and suggested ways that the nature and character of war may change. These various aspects reflect that AI brings a new collective intelligence to the waging of war that thinks fundamentally differently from that of humans alone. This article discusses some implications of using AI to help guide humans in fighting future wars in the Indo-Pacific. The first part of the article examines military AI-enabled DSSs; the second discusses their recent use in the Gaza and Ukraine Wars; the third considers some implications of this initial use of AI-enabled DSS in war; the fourth section looks forward to consider US contingency plans for a hypothetical AI-enabled DSS battle of the Taiwan Straits; the conclusion proposes some steps Indo-Pacific armed forces may need to take to partly address the identified problems.

items.title: Using conversational artificial intelligence to dissect the psychoneuroimmunology of social safety and threat
items.abstract: Human health is profoundly shaped by the quality of our social environments, yet the mechanisms through which social experiences become biologically embedded remain poorly understood. Social Safety Theory (SST) proposes that perceived social safety and threat influence health through neuroendocrine and immune pathways, but it remains unclear which features of social interaction engage these pathways. Here, we argue that conversational artificial intelligence (AI) provides a powerful experimental tool to address this mechanistic gap. Synthetic agents allow researchers to systematically vary core social signals, including responsiveness, reciprocity, empathic cues, agency, and multimodal information, while holding other features of the interaction relatively constant. This controllability creates a unique opportunity to identify which social signals are necessary or sufficient to generate perceived safety or threat and to engage downstream biological responses. Building on SST, we propose a psychoneuroimmunological framework linking experimentally controlled features of synthetic social interaction to neuroendocrine and immune processes and derive testable hypotheses concerning perceived humanness, social-signal strength, and multimodal embodiment. By enabling the causal decomposition of social interaction, conversational AI could help reveal what makes an interaction biologically social and clarify the mechanisms linking social disconnection to health.

items.title: Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for proteins have advanced rapidly, improving structure prediction and design, particularly for de novo binders. However, most evaluations emphasize binding affinity rather than higher-order biological function. We present Bits to Binders, a global competition evaluating de novo binder design in the context of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Teams from 42 countries submitted 12,000 designs of 80-amino acid de novo minibinders targeting human CD20 as CAR binding domains. Designs were screened by pooled CAR-T proliferation, identifying 707 designs exhibiting significant CD20-specific enrichment, with team hit rates from 0.6% to 38.4%. Top-performing candidates were validated as individual constructs, measuring CD20-specific proliferation, expansion, cytokine production, and targeted cell lysis. We identified common design methodologies and factors correlated with DNA synthesis, expression, and target-specific T cell activation which nearly double the success rates when applied as a retrospective filter. We release this dataset as an open resource, with practical recommendations to support more effective AI-driven binder design.

items.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

items.title: VESSI - VLM-Enhanced Support for Surveillance and Investigations
items.abstract: Automated video surveillance analysis has become a critical component of intelligence infrastructures and Law Enforcement agencies. Traditional systems lack the semantic module for comprehensive situational awareness and forensic tasks, limiting their ability to interpret events meaningfully or support post-incident investigations. This slows operational insight and increases the burden on human analysts. Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer promising pathways to bridge this gap. To address this, we propose VLM-Enhanced Support for Surveillance and Investigations (VESSI), a VLM-based framework designed to enhance automated video surveillance analysis through prompt-driven interrogation of video sequences where salient visual features are converted into textual descriptions. We test our framework with four state-of-the-art models. Since most datasets for this task are unlabeled, we also propose the Composite Model Utility Score (CMUS) to assess VLM performance. Experimental results show that our solution substantially improves the analysis capabilities of human operators and enhances the flexibility of automated surveillance systems. In our evaluation, the most reliable model flagged potentially relevant activity in more than 66% of the videos while reducing review time by more than 85%, offering a practical balance between selectivity and efficiency. The model ordering produced by the reference-free CMUS evaluation was reproduced by the normal-video CMUS evaluation and matched the false-positive-rate ordering obtained from 5,909 manually referenced frames. This agreement supports the operational use of the score within the evaluated setting.

items.title: Viewpoint on Functional Coupling and Neural Oscillations in Multisensory Integration
items.abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint article, Jennifer Bizley and Daniel Senkowski share their perspectives on past, present, and future developments in research on the roles of functional coupling and neural oscillations in multisensory integration. Drawing on existing studies, the authors argue that a central finding that has shaped the field is that processing in early sensory cortices is influenced by stimuli from other modalities. This finding challenges the classical view of these areas as strictly unisensory. Advances in brain stimulation methods, high-density neural recordings, and computational and machine learning approaches are propelling the field toward richer datasets, a more mechanistic understanding, and causal tests of how neural oscillations and functional coupling may support multisensory integration. Key controversies include the significance of the individual alpha frequency in multisensory integration, and whether crossmodal interactions in early sensory cortices reflect genuine multisensory interactions or movement-related artifacts. The authors advocate for open-science practices, including preregistration, data sharing, and publicly available analysis code. Looking ahead, the authors anticipate that the implementation of artificial intelligence and the use of large-scale microelectrode arrays will bridge the gap between micro- and macroscale observations by linking circuit-level findings in animals to large-scale human neuroimaging data. They advise young scientists to develop expertise across multiple sensory modalities, pursue unexpected findings, and actively engage with the collaborative multisensory research community. The authors emphasize that multisensory research examining functional coupling and neural oscillations is ecologically valid, full of unanswered questions, and of growing importance in cognitive and clinical neuroscience.
